analysis.one_liner: Made employers cover workers or pay into a new public health plan, funded by broad tax increases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after six days of hearings in the Ways and Means Committee in October 1991, it sat in three House committees without a markup and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill required every employer to enroll its workers and their families in a certified health plan meeting federal standards, or pay a tax (9% of wages, 80% paid by the employer) that would fund a new government health plan, similar to Medicare, for anyone without other coverage. A national commission would cap total health spending and set limits on what hospitals and doctors could be paid. Medicare eligibility would drop from 65 to 60, and preventive services would be added. To pay for it, the bill imposed a surtax of up to 9% on income tax bills, raised the Medicare payroll tax, and raised the wage base subject to that tax to $200,000.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans without health insurance would get coverage through a public plan or through their employer's certified plan. Low-income enrollees would get help paying premiums and cost-sharing. Workers at small businesses, who are least likely to have coverage, would be covered by 1996. Adults aged 60 to 64 would gain Medicare eligibility, and everyone would get new preventive benefits like cancer screenings and well-child care.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must either enroll employees and their families in a qualified health plan or pay a premium tax funding a new public health plan open to anyone not otherwise covered, with all remaining uninsured people automatically enrolled by January 1, 1996 [S2][S3].
Low-income enrollees are eligible for assistance that limits or eliminates their premiums, deductibles, and copayments under the public plan [S2].

Small employers would be covered starting January 1, 1996, and the bill bans carriers from refusing or dropping small-employer plans for any reason other than nonpayment or fraud, requires community rating, and bars discrimination based on health status [S2].

Medicare eligibility would drop by one year per year starting in 1993, reaching age 60 on January 1, 1997, with new coverage for colorectal and breast cancer screening, immunizations, and well-child care [S2].

A national spending limit on health expenditures, growing more slowly each year until it reaches zero growth after 2000, would be enforced by a new Health Care Cost Containment Commission negotiating provider payment ceilings [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that do not provide qualified coverage would pay 80% of a 9% premium tax on their wage base, and their employees would pay the other 20%. All taxpayers would face a surtax reaching 9% of their income tax liability, and workers and the self-employed would pay a higher Medicare payroll tax on wages up to $200,000. Hospitals and doctors would accept payment ceilings under the national spending cap. Individuals who fail to enroll in the public plan when required would owe double premiums retroactively.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, taxpayers, and health care providers

drawbacks.text: The financing is broad and hits working people directly: a surtax of up to 9% of tax liability on individuals and corporations, a higher Medicare payroll tax rate (1.45% rising to 1.65%), and an increased wage base to $200,000 [S2].

The employer premium tax is split 80/20, but the bill also allows employers to charge employees up to 20% of the premium for basic coverage, so many workers would bear part of the cost of a mandate they cannot opt out of [S2][S3].

Coverage would be mandatory: people eligible for the public plan who do not apply by January 1, 1996 would be retroactively enrolled and charged twice the premiums otherwise due unless they show good cause [S2].

The spending caps are blunt: a national expenditure limit and ceilings on what providers may be paid could constrain access or quality if set too tight, and payment rates under the public plan would be shielded from administrative or judicial review [S2][S3].
State benefit mandates would be preempted, so states could not require employer plans to cover services beyond the federal basic package [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded one of the largest possible gains for ordinary people—universal health coverage with a guaranteed basic benefit package and low-income assistance—for one of the largest broad-based tax increases ever proposed, hitting income tax bills, payroll, and employer payrolls at once. Its cost containment system was aggressive and largely untested, and the mandatory-enrollment penalty on individuals was harsh. Whether the trade was worth it depended on whether the spending caps could hold costs down without degrading care, which no one could guarantee. It was a serious, fully specified attempt at universal coverage, not a token bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, got six days of hearings in the Ways and Means Committee in October 1991, but was never reported out or brought to a floor vote, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski, the chairman of the powerful House Ways and Means Committee, introduced the bill on August 2, 1991 with a single Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
It was referred jointly to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor, and to their subcommittees [S5].
The Ways and Means Committee held hearings on six days in October 1991, but the bill was never marked up or reported to the House, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the premium tax and the surtax, along with high earners facing the new income surtax and Medicare wage-base increase, were better off because the bill died. The health insurance industry kept its existing underwriting practices, and hospitals and physicians avoided the national payment ceilings. Americans without health coverage remained without it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, high earners, insurers, and providers

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the record shows only a Democratic chairman and one Democratic cosponsor on one side and no recorded opposition votes; the broader 1991-92 fight over employer mandates divided mostly along party lines, with Republicans and business groups opposed.

industries.note: The bill keeps employer-based private insurance as the primary channel: medium and small employers must buy certified insured plans, creating a near-universal customer base, while large employers may self-insure. At the same time, insurers face guaranteed-issue and community-rating rules, a 50% excise tax on nonconforming plans, and a new public plan competing for everyone outside employer coverage.

A national spending cap with ceilings on provider payment rates, set by a new commission and indexed toward zero growth after 2000, would directly limit what providers are paid for a large share of care. Cost restraint of this kind is the intended benefit to patients and premium payers.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those without health plans
industries.note: Any employer not offering a qualified plan owes a tax of 9% of its wage base (80% share) plus a $100-per-day penalty for failing to file enrollment information. Employers would bear the largest direct cost of the bill.

A surtax of 6% rising to 9% of income tax liability, plus a higher Medicare payroll tax and an increased wage base to $200,000, would fall on upper earners and corporations to fund universal coverage.
